title: PTSD a real problem for cops
article: A special report from the provincial Ombudsman coming Wednesday is opening discussions about Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and its effect on police officers.
"It's an occupation where we see a lot of things the average person doesn't see," said Barrie police Chief Mark Neelin.
In March 2011, the Ombudsman announced the study after more than 30 OPP officers complained about the lack of support in their force after dealing with repeated traumatic situations.
Ombudsman Andre Marin said he may not have "jurisdiction over (municipal) police services" but said the investigation would examine "what the ministry is doing across the province."
Suicide, tragic fatalities, brutal assaults and seeing children injured are all part of the job. And officers don't get to choose which scenario they respond to.
"PTSD is the new terminology, but it's always been around. After the Second World War, we called it shell shock," said Neelin.
Neelin said he'd review the report once it comes out, but said mental wellness of officers is something the Barrie Police Service is already taking seriously.
"We just had a know-your-numbers day where we measured blood pressure and cholesterol levels, so they are aware of where they're at," said Neelin.
And while some residents may think that small-town policing isn't as harsh as in the big city, Neelin said size doesn't matter.
"We're not really a small town anymore. We really are mid-size and everything occurs in Barrie," he said.
To address that, in 2009, the Barrie Police Service created a peer support team.

Const. Wayne Dufour manages the team, and completed his training just two weeks before Constables Dave Edgar and Clayton Speers were slashed with a knife on Bayfield Street by Dennis Melton. Bleeding from the neck, the officers reacted by shooting and killing Melton.
Edgar still has the physical scar from that day, behind his left ear. But it's not something he can see in the mirror each day.
He was only six months on the job when he showed up on Bayfield Street that day. "In a 30-year career, many officers won't see what me and Speers went through that day," said Edgar.
After the shooting, the officers were offered the opportunity to talk with a psychotherapist.
"I'd never been exposed to that before and they had someone lined up for us - if we chose to use it. We both did."
Edgar liked the fact that the option was available to him. It also wasn't something forced on him.
After dealing with feelings of guilt and moving on, Edgar admitted it was tough when almost three years to the day a Coroner's Inquest was held.
"It brought it all back full force. I had to testify graphic details in front of the deceased's family, our peers and our family," said Edgar. "I thought I was done with this."
Aside from having professional help, Edgar added it's also nice to have a peer support group.
"They're not psychotherapists, but they're people we know and we're comfortable talking with them. I can call them outside of work and speak with them confidentially."
"We process things with our five senses. Death has a distinct smell. Burning flesh has a distinct smell."
And every scene will affect each officer differently.
Dufour said officers might have difficulties going certain places if the sights or smells trigger a memory of a tragic incident.
"But if they don't know what they're experiencing is normal, they think if they tell anyone, people will think they're nuts."
Dufour said one Barrie police officer responded to both Edgar's incident and the double homicide at the Travelodge Hotel in May.
"During our career, the calls don't end when we leave the scene. We deal with repetitive trauma or crises, stuff we can't leave behind," said Dufour.
There are 26 officers on the peer support group and, on average, they speak with six officers each month, said Dufour.
Barrie Police Service has taken stress on the job seriously, and created Dufour's position as head of organizational wellness in January.
But it can be a struggle having to prove the value in the program.
"The problem with selling this (as a budget item) is there's nothing tangible to show. We tell (the police board) we need to take a course, they want to know their return on investment."
For Edgar, it's a no-brainer.
"Even if you look at it in terms of budget, it can't be that expensive in terms of the value you get out of it," he said.
